extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties conducting discovery depositions in Board inter partes proceedings (TTAB/practice before the USPTO Board)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules governing how discovery depositions (oral and written) are noticed, taken, and challenged in inter partes proceedings before the Board, including special rules for foreign witnesses, organizations (Rule 30(b)(6)), remote depositions, time limits, and re-depositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposing a foreign party present in the U.S. (37 CFR §2.120(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a foreign party (or its officer, director, managing agent, or other person who consents to testify on its behalf) will be, during a time set for discovery, present within the United States or any territory under U.S. control, such person may be deposed, while in the United States, by oral examination on notice pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(c)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the deposition of a foreign party (or a person who consents to testify for a foreign party) is taken in the United States pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(c)(2), it must be taken in the federal judicial district where the witness resides or is regularly employed, or if the witness neither resides nor is regularly employed in a district, where the witness is at the time of the deposition. (See notes/cases cited, e.g., Rhone-Poulenc; Jonergin.) This option existed even before adoption of §2.120(c)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign person present in U.S. who is a nonparty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed deponent is a foreign person present within the United States but not a party and not willing to appear voluntarily, it may be necessary to secure the deponent's attendance by the procedures set forth in TBMP § 404.03(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonparty foreign domiciliary present in the U.S. cannot simply be noticed like a party and may require subpoena or other procedures; consult TBMP §404.03(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons before whom depositions may be taken (within U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the United States or a territory subject to U.S. jurisdiction, a deposition must be taken before (A) an officer authorized to administer oaths by federal law or by the law in the place of examination; or (B) a person appointed by the court where the action is pending to administer oaths and take testimony (Fed. R. Civ. P. 28(a)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term “officer” includes persons appointed by the court or designated by the parties under Rule 29(a). Discovery depositions in Board inter partes proceedings may be taken before the persons designated by Fed. R. Civ. P. 28. Practically, depositions in the U.S. are usually taken before a court reporter authorized to administer oaths in the jurisdiction. Do not take depositions before a person disqualified by Rule 28(c) (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions in a foreign country (Fed. R. Civ. P. 28(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition may be taken in a foreign country (A) under an applicable treaty or convention; (B) under a letter of request (letter rogatory); (C) on notice, before a person authorized to administer oaths either by U.S. federal law or by the law in the place of examination; or (D) before a person commissioned by the court to administer any necessary oath and take testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A letter of request, commission, or other device must follow the form prescribed by the treaty/convention when applicable. Evidence obtained in response to a letter of request need not be excluded merely because it is not a verbatim transcript or because testimony was not taken under oath. Parties should consult local counsel or the Department of State (Office of Citizens Consular Services) before attempting to take depositions in a foreign country because some countries prohibit or condition taking testimony for use in other countries. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 28(b)(3)-(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification of persons before whom depositions are taken (Fed. R. Civ. P. 28(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition must not be taken before a person who is any party’s relative, employee, or attorney; who is related to or employed by any party’s attorney, or who is financially interested in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the person taking the oath is impartial and not disqualified under Rule 28(c). If the designated officer falls into one of these categories, a different officer or court-appointed person must be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of deposition — general requirements (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who wants to depose a person by oral questions must give reasonable written notice to every other party. The notice must state the time and place of the deposition and, if known, the deponent’s name and address; if the name is unknown, the notice must provide a general description sufficient to identify the person or the class or group to which the person belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether notice is 'reasonable' depends on circumstances. Elements to include are specified in Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1). It is strongly recommended that the deposing party contact the party sought to be deposed well in advance to arrange a mutually convenient time. Closing of discovery period is not a compelling reason to fail to give reasonable notice. See notes and related TBMP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting production of documents at deposition (Rule 34 interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice to a party deponent may be accompanied by a request under Rule 34 to produce documents and tangible things at the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceeding under Rule 34 is appropriate when documents are few, simple, and closely related to the oral examination. The deposing party must allow at least 30 days between the date of the request and the deposition to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 34 (35 days if served by first-class mail or overnight courier). For combining a deposition notice with a Rule 34 request, see TBMP § 406.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to an organization — Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In its notice or subpoena, a party may name as the deponent a corporation, partnership, association, governmental agency, or other entity and must describe with reasonable particularity the matters for examination. The organization must designate one or more officers, directors, or managing agents, or other persons who consent to testify on its behalf, and may set out the matters on which each person will testify. The persons designated must testify about information known or reasonably available to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization speaks through its designated representative(s); a 30(b)(6) designee's answers bind the organization. The organization must prepare designees to give complete, knowledgeable, and binding answers regarding matters known or reasonably available to the organization. It may produce multiple deponents or prepare one who reviews records to become knowledgeable. If a designee is deficient, the organization must provide a substitute and prepare that person. Failure to designate, to appear, or to produce a prepared witness can lead to motions to compel or sanctions; production of an unprepared witness is tantamount to failure to appear. For interplay with Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1) and examples, see TBMP notes and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) depositions for numerical/time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though more than one person may be designated under a Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) notice, for the ten deposition limit under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2)(A)(i) the 30(b)(6) deposition is treated as a single deposition. For the time limitation under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(d)(1) (1 day of 7 hours), the deposition of each designated person under a 30(b)(6) notice is considered a separate deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan depositions strategically: a 30(b)(6) notice counts as one of the ten depositions available, but if multiple designees testify, the seven-hour limit generally applies to each designated person separately. Prior individual testimony by a witness on a topic does not relieve the organization of the duty to designate a 30(b)(6) witness on that topic because individual testimony is not binding on the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and capacity distinctions for natural persons (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1) deposition of a natural person seeks information regarding that individual’s personal knowledge. Taking the deposition of a party’s officer, director, or managing agent in his or her individual capacity probes that person's personal knowledge; taking the deposition in his or her organizational capacity (or as a 30(b)(6) designee) elicits testimony attributable to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An employee or agent who does not qualify as an officer, director, or managing agent is not subject to deposition by notice under 30(b)(1) and must be treated as a non-party witness (i.e., may require subpoena). It is possible to depose the same person both in an individual capacity and in an organizational capacity; treat each capacity distinctly for use at trial and discovery purposes. See TBMP § 412.06(a) for high-level officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote depositions — telephone/video and place of deposition (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: On stipulation of the parties, or on motion granted by the Board, a deposition may be taken or attended by telephone or other remote means (e.g., video conferencing). For purposes of the rules, the deposition takes place where the deponent answers the questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deposition taken by remote means is regarded as taken in the federal judicial district and at the place where the witness answers. A discovery deposition taken by remote means must be transcribed if submitted as evidence at trial. Courts favor granting telephonic/remote depositions when appropriate; parties may stipulate or request Board order to resolve travel conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration limit for depositions (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise stipulated or ordered, a deposition is limited to 1 day of 7 hours. Only actual deposition time counts against the presumptive limit; reasonable lunch and other breaks do not count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 30(b)(6) depositions, each designated person's examination is considered a separate deposition for durational limits. A party seeking more time must show good cause consistent with Rule 26(b)(2). Additional time must be allowed if the deponent or other person impedes or delays examination, or other circumstances (power outage, health emergency). Orders directing shorter depositions or limited periods on several days are permitted. Parties should try to accommodate scheduling to avoid motion practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-deposing a witness (leave required) (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person has already been deposed in the case, a party must seek leave of the Board to take a second deposition if the parties have not stipulated to a second deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting or denying leave is at the Board's discretion, guided by Rule 26(b)(2). The Board will consider whether the discovery sought is unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, obtainable from another source more convenient/less burdensome/less expensive, whether the seeking party had ample opportunity previously to obtain the information, and whether the burden or expense outweighs the likely benefit. Exceptions: temporary recesses to gather additional materials do not trigger leave requirement; consider remote means to avoid travel costs for resumption. See cited cases for examples where leave denied due to duplicative topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions on written questions — filing, notice and timing (37 CFR §2.124)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition upon written questions must be taken in the manner prescribed by 37 CFR § 2.124. A party desiring to take such a deposition shall serve notice upon each adverse party and shall file a copy of the notice (but not copies of the questions) with the Board. The notice shall state the name and address, if known, of the person whose deposition is to be taken; if unknown, provide a general description to identify the person or class. Every notice must be accompanied by the name or descriptive title of the officer before whom the deposition is to be taken, and the notice served on adverse parties must be accompanied by the written questions to be propounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery depositions on written questions must be noticed and taken during the discovery period (37 CFR §2.120(a)(3)); it is recommended to initiate the procedure early. For the place of deposition, consult TBMP §404.03. When using written questions, serve the questions with the notice on adverse parties, but file only the notice (not the questions) with the Board. Follow the formalities required by 37 CFR §2.124(d)(1) and §2.124(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement — depositions must be taken during discovery period
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be both noticed and taken during the discovery period (37 CFR §2.120(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because depositions on written questions or oral examinations must occur within the discovery period, parties should initiate depositions early in their discovery window. The Board has discretion on scheduling and whether to suspend unrelated discovery activities pending a proposed deposition on written questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization's obligation to prepare 30(b)(6) designees
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization served with a 30(b)(6) notice must pick and produce persons that have knowledge of the subject matter identified and must prepare those persons so they can give complete, knowledgeable, and binding answers as to matters known or reasonably available to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no current employee has knowledge of a noticed matter, the organization is nonetheless obliged to prepare a designee from past records, past employees, or other sources reasonably available. If the designee is inadequately prepared, the organization must supply a substitute and further prepare witnesses; failing to do so can lead to motions to compel, orders for additional deposition time, or sanctions, and may require payment of costs for second depositions. Cases cited (United Technologies, Tulip Computers, etc.) illustrate consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation — arrange deposition scheduling in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is strongly recommended that the deposing party contact the party sought to be deposed (or that party's officer/designee) well in advance of the proposed deposition to arrange a mutually convenient time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early communications reduce scheduling conflicts, avoid last-minute motions, and help preserve the reasonableness of notice. The Board expects parties to make reasonable accommodations to obviate the need for motion practice regarding deposition time limits or scheduling conflicts.
